title: The virgin birth and the limits of sight
source_text: Εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς ταυτολογῶν μετὰ τὸ πολλὰ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰπεῖν καὶ χλευάσαι τὴν ἐκ παρθένου γέννησιν τοῦ θεοῦ, πρὸς ἣν κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν ἀπηντήσαμεν, φησίν· εἰ δ᾿ ἐβούλετο πνεῦμα ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ καταπέμψαι, τί ἐδεῖτο εἰς γυναικὸς γαστέρα ἐμπνεῖν; ἐδύνατο γὰρ ἤδη πλάσσειν ἀνθρώπους εἰδὼς καὶ τούτῳ περιπλάσαι σῶμα καὶ μὴ τὸ ἴδιον πνεῦμα εἰς τοσοῦτον μίασμα ἐμβαλεῖν· οὕτως μέν τ᾿ ἂν οὐδ᾿ ἠπιστεῖτο, εἰ ἄνωθεν εὐθὺς ἔσπαρτο. καὶ ταῦτ᾿ εἶπεν, ἐπεὶ μὴ εἶδε τὴν παρθενικὴν καὶ καθαρὰν γέννησιν καὶ ἀπὸ μηδεμιᾶς φθορᾶς τοῦ μέλλοντος ὑπηρετήσασθαι τῇ ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίᾳ σώματος. οἴεται δὲ ὁ τὸν Στωϊκὸν λόγον ἐκτιθέμενος καὶ μὴ προσποιούμενος τὰ περὶ ἀδιαφόρων μεμαθηκέναι εἰς μίασμα ἐμβεβλῆσθαι τὴν θείαν φύσιν καὶ μεμιάσθαι εἴτε γενομένην ἐν γυναικὸς σώματι, ἕως περιπλασθῇ αὐτῇ τὸ σῶμα, εἴτε σῶμα ἀνειληφυῖαν· παραπλήσιόν τι ποιῶν τοῖς οἰομένοις τὰς αὐγὰς τοῦ ἡλίου μιαίνεσθαι ἐν τοῖς βορβόροις καὶ τοῖς δυσώδεσι σώμασι καὶ μὴ μένειν κἀκεῖ καθαράς. καὶ εἰ κατὰ τὴν Κέλσου δὲ ὑπόθεσιν χωρὶς γεννήσεως περιεπλάσατο τὸ σῶμα τῷ Ἰησοῦ. (οὐκ) εὐθὺς ἂν οἱ βλέποντες τὸ σῶμα ἐπίστευον ὅτι οὐκ ἀπὸ γεννήσεως ἦν· οὐδὲ γὰρ τὸ βλεπόμενον ἀπαγγέλλει καὶ τὴν φύσιν, ὅθεν γεγένηται. οἷον εἰ καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν μέλι ἦν τι μὴ ἀπὸ μελισσῶν, οὐκ ἂν τοῦτό τις ἀπήγγελλεν ἀπὸ τῆς γεύσεως ἢ τῆς ὄψεως. ὅτι μὴ ἀπὸ μελισσῶν ἐστιν· ὡς οὐδὲ τὸ ἀπὸ μελισσῶν δείκνυσι τῇ αἰσθήσει τὴν ἀρχὴν, ἀλλ᾿ ἡ πεῖρα δείκνυσιν ὅτι τοῦτ᾿ μελισσῶν ἐστιν. οὕτω δὲ καὶ ἡ πεῖρα διδάσκει ὅτι ἀπὸ ἀμπέλου ὁ οἶνος· οὐ γὰρ ἀναφέρει ἡ γεῦσις τὸ ἀπὸ ἀμπέλου. τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον τοίνυν τὸ αἰσθητὸν σῶμα οὐκ ἀπαγγέλλει τὸν τρόπον τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. προσαχθήσῃ δὲ τῷ λεγομένῳ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν οὐρανοῖς, ὧν τῆς ὑποστάσεως καὶ τῆς λαμπρότητος αἰσθόμεθα βλέποντες ἀλλ᾿ οὐ δή που ἡ αἴσθησις ἡμῖν ὑποβάλλει, πότερον γενητὰ ἢ ἀγένητά ἐστιν. αἱρέσεις γοῦν καὶ περὶ τούτων συνέστησαν· ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ λέγοντες αὐτὰ γενητὰ οὐχ ὁμονοοῦσι περὶ τοῦ πῶς ἐστι γενητά· οὐδὲ γὰρ ὑποβάλλει ἡ αἴσθησις αὐτῶν. κἂν βιασάμενος ὁ λόγος εὕρῃ ὅτι γενητά ἐστι. περὶ τοῦ τίνα τρόπον γεγένηται.
pass_a_gloss: Then next (ἑξῆς), repeating himself (ταυτολογέω) after saying many things in the earlier parts (ἀνωτέρω) and mocking (χλευάζω) the birth (γέννησις) of God from a virgin (παρθένος), to which according to what was possible for us we replied (ἀπαντάω), he says: but if he wished to send down a spirit from himself, why did he need (δέομαι) to breathe into (ἐμπνέω) a woman's womb (γαστήρ)? For he was able, already knowing (οἶδα) how to mould (πλάσσω) men, also for this one to mould around (περιπλάσσω) a body and not cast (ἐμβάλλω) his own spirit into so great a pollution (μίασμα); thus indeed he would not even be disbelieved (ἀπιστέω), if from above (ἄνωθεν) at once (εὐθύς) he had been sown (σπείρω). And he said these things since he did not see/know (εἶδε) the virginal (παρθενικός) and pure (καθαρός) birth, and from no corruption (φθορά), of the body about to serve (ὑπηρετέω) the salvation (σωτηρία) of men. And he who sets out (ἐκτίθημι) the Stoic doctrine (λόγος) and not pretending (προσποιέομαι) to have learned the things about indifferents (ἀδιάφορα) thinks the divine nature (θεία φύσις) has been cast into pollution and been polluted (μιαίνω), whether having come to be in a woman's body, until the body was moulded around it, or having taken up (ἀναλαμβάνω) a body; doing something similar (παραπλήσιον) to those thinking the rays (αὐγαί) of the sun are polluted in the mires (βόρβορος) and the ill-smelling (δυσώδης) bodies and do not remain (μένω) pure even there. And if according to Celsus's supposition (ὑπόθεσις) without birth the body was moulded around for Jesus, (not) at once would those seeing the body have believed that it was not from birth; for not even what is seen announces (ἀπαγγέλλω) also the nature whence it has come to be. As, if by supposition there were some honey (μέλι) not from bees (μέλισσα), no one would announce this from taste (γεῦσις) or sight (ὄψις), that it is not from bees; as not even that from bees shows to sense (αἴσθησις) its origin (ἀρχή), but experience (πεῖρα) shows that this is from bees. So also experience teaches that wine is from the vine (ἄμπελος); for taste does not refer back (ἀναφέρω) to its being from the vine. In the same way then the sensible (αἰσθητός) body does not announce the manner of its subsistence (ὑπόστασις). You will be brought (προσάγω) to what is said from the things in the heavens, of whose subsistence and brightness (λαμπρότης) we perceive (αἰσθάνομαι) seeing (them), but surely (δή που) sense does not suggest (ὑποβάλλω) to us whether they are generated (γενητός) or ungenerated (ἀγένητος). Schools/sects (αἱρέσεις) at any rate also about these have arisen (συνίστημι); but even those saying they are generated do not agree (ὁμονοέω) about how they are generated; for sense of them does not suggest (it), even if reason (λόγος), forcing (βιάζομαι), find that they are generated, about in what manner they have come to be.
pass_b_english: Next, repeating himself after saying a great deal in the earlier parts and mocking the birth of God from a virgin, to which we have replied as well as we could, he says: “If he wanted to send down a spirit from himself, why did he need to breathe it into a woman’s womb? For since he already knew how to form men, he could have formed a body around this one too, and not cast his own spirit into such great pollution. In that way he would not even have been disbelieved, if he had been begotten straight from above.”

He said this because he did not know the virgin and pure birth, without any corruption, of the body that was to serve the salvation of men. And though he sets out the Stoic doctrine, he shows no sign of having learned what it teaches about things indifferent, and thinks that the divine nature was cast into pollution and was polluted, whether by coming to be in a woman’s body until a body was formed around it, or by taking up a body. He does much the same as those who think that the rays of the sun are polluted in mire and in foul-smelling bodies, and do not remain pure even there.

Even if, on Celsus’s supposition, the body had been formed for Jesus without birth, those who saw the body would not at once have believed that it did not come from birth. For what is seen does not also announce the nature from which it came. Suppose, for instance, there were some honey not made by bees: no one could tell from tasting it or looking at it that it was not from bees. Just so, honey from bees does not show its origin to the senses; experience shows that it comes from bees. So too experience teaches that wine comes from the vine; for the taste does not tell us that it comes from the vine. In the same way, then, the body that is perceived does not announce how it came into being.

You will be brought to accept what I say by the example of the heavenly bodies. We perceive their existence and their brightness when we see them; but sense surely does not suggest to us whether they have come into being or are without origin. In fact schools of thought have arisen about these very things; and even those who say they have come into being do not agree on how they came into being. For sense does not suggest to them in what way they came into being, even if reason, pressing hard, finds that they did come into being.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words from ‘If he wanted’ to ‘straight from above’ are in double quotation marks. ἔσπαρτο (lit. ‘had been sown’) rendered ‘had been begotten’. Celsus’s earlier mockery of the virgin birth and Origen’s reply refer to Book 1 (1.28-39); no Scripture is quoted in this chapter, and none is cited. μὴ προσποιούμενος τὰ περὶ ἀδιαφόρων μεμαθηκέναι is ironic: one who expounds Stoic teaching yet behaves as if he had never learned its doctrine that bodily things are ‘indifferent’ (neither good nor bad, and so not defiling); rendered ‘he shows no sign of having learned’. Koetschau supplies (οὐκ) before εὐθὺς ἂν οἱ βλέποντες; followed. The TEI’s τοῦτ᾿ μελισσῶν lacks ἀπό; read as τοῦτ᾿ ἀπὸ μελισσῶν. ὡς οὐδέ rendered ‘Just so’ (a parallel, not a new step). ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν οὐρανοῖς rendered ‘by the example of the heavenly bodies’. γενητά / ἀγένητα rendered ‘have come into being’ / ‘are without origin’. The last two clauses (κἂν βιασάμενος ὁ λόγος εὕρῃ ὅτι γενητά ἐστι. περὶ τοῦ τίνα τρόπον γεγένηται) are badly punctuated in the TEI; περὶ τοῦ τίνα τρόπον is taken with ὑποβάλλει (‘sense does not suggest ... in what way’), and the sentence is reordered into natural English without adding to it. ‘Schools of thought’ renders αἱρέσεις (philosophical schools, not heresies).
6.73: 'In the same way, honey from bees' to 'Just so' (ὡς οὐδέ, avoids repeating 'In the same way' two sentences later)
6.73: 'by the heavenly bodies' to 'by the example of the heavenly bodies' (ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν οὐρανοῖς: they are the illustration, not the agent)
